items.followUp: Define a compound and state how it differs from an element.

rubric.why: A correct definition identifies an element as a pure substance made of one kind of atom that cannot be decomposed chemically.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete definition; 1 mark for identifying it as a pure substance made of one kind of atom or stating that it cannot be decomposed chemically.

rubric.why: Metals are one of the three kinds of elements and are generally good conductors of heat and electricity.
rubric.description: Describes metals as a kind of element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming metals and giving a suitable characteristic or example.

rubric.why: Non-metals are another kind of element and are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
rubric.description: Describes non-metals as a kind of element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming non-metals and giving a suitable characteristic or example.

rubric.why: Metalloids have properties intermediate between metals and non-metals.
rubric.description: Identifies metalloids as a kind of element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming metalloids and stating that their properties are intermediate, or giving a suitable example.

modelAnswer: An element is a pure substance made up of only one kind of atom and cannot be decomposed into simpler substances by chemical means.
Elements are classified into three kinds:
Metals are generally lustrous and good conductors of heat and electricity; examples are iron and copper.
Non-metals are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity; examples are oxygen and sulphur.
Metalloids have properties intermediate between metals and non-metals; silicon is an example.

items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and give one example of a compound containing it.

rubric.why: A covalent bond forms when atoms share electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a covalent bond is formed by sharing one or more pairs of electrons between atoms.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond consists of one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one pair of electrons is shared; accept a correct example such as H₂.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond consists of two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that two pairs of electrons are shared; accept a correct example such as O₂.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond consists of three shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that three pairs of electrons are shared; accept a correct example such as N₂.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond is formed by sharing one pair of electrons, for example, H₂.
A double covalent bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons, for example, O₂.
A triple covalent bond is formed by sharing three pairs of electrons, for example, N₂.

items.followUp: State the main conclusions Rutherford drew from the gold foil experiment.

rubric.why: The experiment involved directing alpha particles at a very thin sheet of gold.
rubric.description: Identifies the particles and gold foil used.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing alpha particles directed at a thin gold foil.

rubric.why: A radioactive source and shielding produced a narrow beam of alpha particles for the experiment.
rubric.description: Describes how the alpha-particle beam was produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning a radioactive alpha source and a narrow beam or its shielding/collimation.

rubric.why: The screen showed where alpha particles struck after passing through or being deflected by the foil.
rubric.description: Describes detection of the scattered particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a fluorescent, such as zinc sulphide, screen detected the particles.

accept: most alpha particles passed straight through
rubric.why: Most alpha particles passed through the foil without deflection.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that most alpha particles passed straight through without deflection.

accept: very few alpha particles bounced back
rubric.why: A small number were deflected, and a very small number returned or bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for reporting that some particles were deflected and/or very few bounced back.

modelAnswer: A narrow beam of alpha particles from a radioactive source was directed at a very thin gold foil.
A fluorescent zinc sulphide screen around the foil detected the alpha particles by producing flashes where they struck.
Observations:
Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection.
A few alpha particles were deflected, while a very few bounced back.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature and humidity affect the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: Evaporation is the escape of particles from a liquid's surface into the vapour state below the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining evaporation as a surface change from liquid to vapour that occurs below the boiling point.

rubric.why: Higher temperature gives surface particles more kinetic energy, increasing evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing temperature increases the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: A larger exposed surface allows more liquid particles to escape at the same time.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of surface area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing the exposed surface area increases the rate.

rubric.why: Moving air carries vapour away, while low humidity allows more vapour to enter the air.
rubric.description: Explains the effects of wind and humidity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly explaining the effect of wind or humidity; the full answer should mention both.

modelAnswer: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface at a temperature below its boiling point.
Higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation because more particles have enough energy to escape.
A larger surface area increases the rate because more particles are exposed at the surface.
Higher wind speed increases evaporation by carrying vapour away; low humidity also increases evaporation because the air can take up more vapour.

items.followUp: Distinguish between a saturated solution and an unsaturated solution at a given temperature.

rubric.why: An unsaturated solution contains less solute than the maximum amount that can dissolve at that temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it can dissolve more sodium thiosulphate at the stated temperature.

rubric.why: The example must apply the definition to sodium thiosulphate.
rubric.description: Gives the sodium thiosulphate example for an unsaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a sodium thiosulphate solution to which more solute can still be added and dissolved at that temperature.

rubric.why: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution can normally hold at that temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it contains more dissolved sodium thiosulphate than the saturated amount at that temperature.

rubric.why: Careful cooling of a hot saturated solution can produce a supersaturated solution that may crystallise when disturbed or seeded.
rubric.description: Gives the sodium thiosulphate example for a supersaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a hot saturated sodium thiosulphate solution cooled carefully, ideally noting that it is unstable or crystallises on disturbance.

modelAnswer: An unsaturated solution contains less solute than the maximum amount that can dissolve at a given temperature, so it can dissolve more sodium thiosulphate at that temperature.
A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution normally holds at the same temperature.
For example, an unsaturated sodium thiosulphate solution can dissolve more solute.
A hot saturated sodium thiosulphate solution, cooled carefully without crystallisation, becomes supersaturated; it may crystallise if disturbed or seeded.

items.followUp: Define valency and give the valencies of oxygen and carbon.

rubric.why: Valency expresses the combining capacity of an atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining valency as the combining capacity of an atom or the number of bonds it forms.

rubric.why: Examples demonstrate how valency is assigned to elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correct element–valency examples, such as hydrogen 1 and oxygen 2.

modelAnswer: Valency is the combining capacity of an atom, or the number of bonds it can form.
Examples: hydrogen has valency 1, oxygen has valency 2, and carbon has valency 4.

items.followUp: Write the chemical formulae of carbon dioxide and calcium chloride.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for H₂O.

rubric.why: Sodium hydroxide, also called caustic soda, has the formula NaOH.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for NaOH.
